title: Infinite complexity of machines
content_html:
Infinite complexity of machines

Traditionally, a machine is defined as a system of parts working together to perform a function. It is mechanistic, in that it is describable in terms of cause and effect, whilst being finite in components, structure, and operations. Philosophically and mathematically, a machine implies bounded complexity: it can be specified, built, or simulated, even if it is very large.

“Infinite complexity” could mean several things: the machine has an unending number of components, it requires endless steps to function, and its description cannot be compressed into a finite rule (like Chaitin’s Ω or random sequences). It demonstrates emergent infinity: no finite model can capture its full behaviour.

If the system is infinite in extent (e.g. every cogwheel spawns more cogwheels without end), it ceases to be a “machine” in the ordinary sense, because machines are human constructs, bounded in design. If it is infinite in behaviour (never-ending recursion or uncomputable processes), it becomes closer to an organism, environment, or cosmos than a machine. In computability theory: a “machine” like a Turing machine is defined with a finite set of rules but can generate unbounded processes. Infinity emerges from finiteness.

A machine with infinite complexity would be indistinguishable from the universe itself, no longer separable as an “instrument. If you insist on the classical definition, an infinitely complex machine is a contradiction - it stops being a machine. If you relax the definition, “machine” becomes metaphor for any system of interrelations, including the brain, ecosystems, or even the cosmos. So an infinitely complex machine cannot truly be called a machine in the mechanical sense. Instead, it becomes indistinguishable from nature or mind - an open-ended system.

The human brain is finite in matter (≈86 billion neurons, trillions of synapses), but functionally, it seems unbounded because of a combinatorial explosion of possible firing patterns, plasticity (wiring changes in architecture with experience) and emergent dynamics (oscillations, synchrony, chaos). This means the brain behaves as though it were infinite, even though physically finite.

In the Select – Change – Reconstruct framework of memory, selection filters infinite sensory input into bounded memories. Memories are plastic, reconsolidated, endlessly reinterpreted, and each act of recall creates something new, not a static copy. In this way, memory behaves like an open-ended system: not a closed machine, but a process of infinite reworking. Like an “infinite machine,” memory is never finished; it has no final state.

Substrate, Emergence, Experience

Consciousness can be thought of as a boundless process, it appears unbounded because it can turn inward (self-reflection) or outward (world-reflection), and can imagine infinities (numbers, space, time) without limit. Yet it arises from a bounded neural substrate. This mirrors the infinite machine paradox: the finite (neurons, circuits) → the unbounded (experience, thought). The “machine” dissolves into process, just as the universe dissolves into unbounded spacetime. So if we stick to strict mechanistic definitions: yes, the brain is a machine. But if we acknowledge emergent infinity, the brain is machine-like only at the bottom level. At the level of memory and consciousness, it transcends machine-ness, it becomes what might be called an infinite machine: bounded in substance, unbounded in process. Just as a machine of infinite complexity ceases to be “just a machine,” memory and consciousness cease to be “just brain functions” - ==they become open-ended processes indistinguishable from nature itself.==
